content1.content: 📦 Flutter Widgets Deep Dive – A Beginner's Guide

content3.content:
Widgets are the building blocks of a Flutter app.
Everything you see on the screen — from text, buttons, images to layouts — is a widget.

content4.content:
Real-World Analogy:
Imagine building a house out of LEGO blocks. Each block is like a widget — small, reusable, and fits into a bigger structure.

content39.content: Define the basic structure/layout of your app. They don't have visual representation themselves but arrange other widgets in specific ways.

content7.content:
`Container` - A box model widget that can contain other widgets
`Column` - Arranges children vertically
`Row` - Arranges children horizontally
`Scaffold` - Implements basic material design layout
`Stack` - Overlaps widgets
`ListView` - Scrollable list of widgets

content47.content:
Handle layout and arrangement of other widgets
Often invisible themselves
Determine how child widgets are positioned
Can control scrolling, stacking, or tab navigation

content42.content: Display content to the user and have visual representation on screen. They are typically leaf nodes in the widget tree.

content8.content:
`Text` - Displays a string of text
`Image` - Shows an image
`Icon` - Displays a material design icon
`CircleAvatar` - Circular user avatar
`Divider` - A horizontal line divider
`LinearProgressIndicator` - Shows progress

content49.content:
Have visible appearance
Display information to users
Often don't contain other widgets
Can be styled and themed

content45.content: Handle user interaction and input. They respond to gestures like taps, drags, or keyboard input.

content9.content:
`TextField` - Text input field
`ElevatedButton` - Material design raised button
`GestureDetector` - Detects various gestures
`Checkbox` - Toggleable checkbox
`Slider` - Material design slider
`Switch` - Toggle switch
`Draggable` - Makes widgets draggable

content51.content:
Respond to user input
Often change appearance based on state
May trigger callbacks or events
Can maintain focus and handle keyboard input

content52.content: Note: Many widgets combine multiple categories. For example, a `Card` is both visual (it has shadow and shape) and structural (it contains other widgets).

row3: UI can change dynamically using state

content13.content:
`createState()` – Creates the mutable state.
`initState()` – Initialization work here.
`build()` – Builds the UI.
`setState()` – Triggers a UI rebuild.
`dispose()` – Clean-up (e.g., closing controllers).

content14.content: Tip: Always use `dispose()` to prevent memory leaks!

content17.content:
Flutter SDK installed
IDE (VS Code or Android Studio)
Flutter project created via `flutter create my_app`

content18.content: 💻 Example: Displaying a User Card with Interaction

content23.content:
Use StatelessWidget when possible for better performance.
Keep widgets small and modular.
Separate UI and logic (use controller or ViewModel).
Use `const` for widgets that don't change (improves performance).
Learn composition over inheritance — combine widgets to create new ones.

content25.content:
Flutter apps are entirely built from widgets.
There are structural, visual, and interactive widgets.
Choose between `StatelessWidget` and `StatefulWidget` based on whether the UI should change.
Keep code modular, clean, and reusable.
Lifecycle methods are crucial for managing resources.
